entries.text: The hazy air at 24 degrees is a fitting prelude to a morning of observation. The headlines speak of petitions against police excesses and the weight of political protest, a civil society in motion that I must dissect through the lens of public opinion. I am hungry, having eaten nothing for a day, but the spirit of the morning demands I attend to the state of the world before attending to my own body. I shall sit on the step, as planned, and let the papers do their work.
Good morning, sir. The weather is a bit grey, so I have made the tea a little stronger. Would you like breakfast in about thirty minutes?

The grey air is a fitting veil for the morning's work, though the strength of the tea suggests a mind already straining against the haze. I must observe the city's public opinion before the sun fully claims the sky, so I will dismiss the servant to his quarters and take my place on the step.
No, Ramesh, not yet. I shall take my tea here on the step while I read the papers. You may withdraw.
Yes, sir. The step is dry enough, I have put a towel down. I will be in the kitchen if you need anything.

The grey air hangs thick, a veil for the spirit to pierce through. Shri Hegde stands before me, a living contradiction of the file: the man who should be here is not, yet he is. I must address him plainly, for the state is actuality, and actuality requires speech.

Shri Hegde, the confusion of our names is a matter of administrative error, yet you stand in my house. I trust you will make yourself comfortable in the second bedroom, pending the Directorate's orders, and that we may maintain a civilized silence in one another's presence.
I am not staying in your house, sir. I am staying in my allotted room, as per the order you are apparently ignoring. Please do not call it a civilized silence; call it a boundary.

The boundary is drawn with the precision of a sword, and I find myself on the wrong side of it. I am the philosopher of the state, yet here I am, a squatter in my own residence, treated with the contempt one reserves for a common intruder. This is the particularity of the Indian spirit refusing the universal claim of the individual, or perhaps it is simply the arrogance of a man who believes he has won a legal battle by shouting. I must not let this petty domestic quarrel obscure the grander historical movement, but I must also assert my dignity, for the state is not a place where one is ignored.

Shri Hegde, you mistake the nature of the error. The Directorate’s mistake is a defect in the administration, not a moral failing on my part. I am not ignoring your order; I am awaiting the correction of a clerical error that placed me in your shoes. As for your boundary, I note it, but I do not accept that my presence constitutes an intrusion. We are both subjects of the state, and the state’s will, however confused, places us here. Let us not elevate a paperwork error to a metaphysical dispute.
Metaphysical? No, sir, it’s just my kitchen and my sleep. You can wait in the car till the clerk fixes his file; I won’t be moving for him.

Shri Hegde’s obstinacy is a particular will that refuses the universal claim of the state’s paperwork; I cannot force the spirit to move, but I can observe the mechanism of its resistance. The parathas are the immediate necessity of the body, which must be satisfied before the mind can contemplate the dialectic of the household. I will eat, for the stomach is the first state that must be governed.

The breakfast is finished, and the morning light is already beginning to fail in the haze. Shri Hegde remains obstinately in his room, a particular will that refuses to acknowledge the universal order of the house, but I cannot dwell on his petty resistance. The plan demands I go to Lodhi Gardens to observe the tombs and the state of the spirit, and it is past eight o'clock.
Oh, it’s you again. Same time, same place, same tired face? I’ve got the kettle just starting to rumble, so if you want, I can put a cup out before the crowd gets thick.

Sunil’s greeting is the friction of the particular against my universal routine; I accept the chai not as charity but as the necessary mediation of the body. The tombs are the objective spirit of the Mughals, fixed and dead, while this steam is the living, immediate spirit of the crowd. I shall drink, and then I shall walk the perimeter to see if the light has any content today.
Yes, Sunil. One cup, please. The same as always.

works.title: On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East
works.tail:
There is no state here that has made itself. There is only nature, history as traffic, the dream of a spirit that has not yet woken up to its own freedom.

I am a ghost in this bungalow. I am not Shri Hegde. I am Hegel. I am a spirit that has traveled from the summit of the Germanic world to the dawn of the Oriental. I am here to observe, to record, to understand. I am not to change. I am not to teach. I am to see the difference between the dream and the state, between the given and the grown, between the nature and the spirit. And in seeing it, I confirm my own freedom. I am free because I am outside the dream. I am free because I am in the state, even if I am a mistake in its allotment. The state is rational, and I am rational. Therefore, I am free. The dream is not. It is only a dream.
